articles.title: Russia still has 50 Kinzhal missiles after pausing production, HUR claims
articles.body:
Russia still has about 50 Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles in its arsenal, despite pausing production of the munition in order to improve its accuracy, Ukraine's Military Intelligence (HUR) has claimed.
The Kinzhal is a modified version of the Iskander ballistic missile, which is launched by specially modified MiG-31K interceptor jets. Over the course of the full-scale war they have regularly been used to attack Ukraine.
"As of July 2026, the Russian Federation has about 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles and about 50 North Korean ballistic missiles of the KN-23 series, including the KN-24 and KN-30 variants," HUR said in a statement to Ukrainska Pravda.
Leaked Russian documents obtained by Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi revealed each Kinzhal costs around $4.5 million to produce. The documents also said Russia had planned to produce 144 units in 2025.
Production of the Kinzhal has been suspended since April 2026. The accuracy of the munition had been negatively affected by Ukrainian jamming and GPS spoofing, according to aviation industry expert Arkady Dotsenko.
"When we put up our EW (electronic warfare) wall, of 59 launched Kinzhals, only one landed. All the rest were suppressed," one commander of a Ukrainian electronic warfare unit told the Kyiv Independent in April.
Russia has redirected resources from Kinzhal production toward producing other missile types, HUR claims.
"Reorienting production resources to other missile systems allows Russia to maintain necessary production rates and ensure the regular use of missiles against Ukraine," it said in their statement.

articles.title: Romania destroys drone near offshore gas project, blames Russia
articles.body:
(AFP Photo)
A Romanian F-16 fighter jet on Aug. 20 destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project, with Romania's president blaming Russia for the latest incident involving the NATO member bordering Ukraine.
Unauthorized drone activity has become increasingly frequent in recent months across eastern European countries as Ukraine fights off a Russian invasion launched in 2022, with both countries increasingly relying on drone warfare.
In the latest incident, the drone that was destroyed was "loaded with explosives" and did not originate from Ukraine, Defense Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook.
"I strongly condemn the escalation of such irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation," Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on X.
The drone was spotted at 6:28 am local time (0328 GMT) by a commercial vessel, hundreds of meters from the offshore gas project Neptun Deep and 80 nautical miles east of the Black Sea city of Constanta, according to a press release from the defense ministry.
Two Romanian F-16 aircraft were deployed to respond, and one of them destroyed it.
Hundreds of people are currently working at Neptun Deep, according to the government. Neptun Deep is due to start production in 2027.
NATO has shot down four aerial drones in Romania recently, with the latest incident happening during last weekend.
The eastern European country also reported an aerial drone crash on Aug. 20 following Russian strikes on Ukraine.
It fell in an unpopulated area four kilometers (2.5 miles) northeast of the village of Grindu in eastern Romania, close to the border.
No casualties were reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Aug. 20 urged a global response to Moscow's "escalation" of the four-year war after Russian bombardments killed at least 16 people in Kiev and surrounding areas overnight.

articles.title: 'We will tear you to pieces': Indian general warns Erdogan about pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan
articles.body:
Retired Indian Maj.-Gen. Gagan Deep Bakshi warned that the growing alignment among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan could pose a strategic threat to India, while stressing that New Delhi would not sacrifice its ties with Iran to accommodate Israel’s security concerns.
Speaking to the New Delhi-based network, Republic World, Bakshi argued that the emergence of what he calls a "Sunni NATO" in the Middle East is a source of strategic concern for India.
At the same time, he sent a clear message to Israel: The alliance between the two countries is important, but New Delhi will not give up its interests with Iran simply because of the war between Jerusalem and Tehran.
According to Bakshi, the agreement that took shape in Mecca among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has created a new regional reality from India's perspective. "A Sunni NATO comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has been established in the Middle East, in Mecca, and that is a serious cause for concern," he said.
Bakshi stressed that, from India's perspective, Shi'ite Iran serves as an important counterweight to Pakistan.
Iran as a counterweight to Pakistan
"We very much need Shi'ite Iran to be on our side because Pakistan is our primary security headache. China may be the main threat, but together with it, Pakistan is our biggest security headache," he said.
Bakshi compared the threat Iran represents in Israel's eyes with that posed by Pakistan from India's perspective.
"Iran does not have even a single nuclear bomb, and yet it is perceived as an existential threat to Israel. And what about Pakistan? A fundamentalist, jihadist Islamic state that possesses 180 nuclear warheads," he claimed.
He added that India had not seen Israel display similar concern over Pakistan's nuclear arsenal.
"We have not seen Israel losing sleep over the bombs in Pakistan's hands because they are considered a threat only to India," he said.
According to Bakshi, the rapprochement between Ankara and Islamabad is not merely theoretical. He cited Turkish assistance to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, claiming that Turkey supplied it with nearly 1,000 unmanned aerial vehicles and helped operate them.
"This was already a 'Sunni NATO,' with or without an agreement. Turkey and Pakistan are already in an undeclared practical alliance," he said.
Bakshi also noted that during the confrontation, Turkey sent a warship to the port of Karachi, arguing that this was another expression of the close security ties between the two countries.
"Turkey has the largest army in NATO," he said, while questioning its ability to intervene directly in a war between India and Pakistan because of the geographical distance.
According to Bakshi, any Turkish force attempting to come to Pakistan's aid would have to travel through the Mediterranean Sea and the Arabian Sea.
"The Indian Navy can tear apart any Turkish armada that tries to come to Pakistan's aid," he said.
India will not sacrifice its interests with Iran
A central part of Bakshi's remarks was directed squarely at Israel. He stressed that India views Israel as a friend, but would not agree to subordinate its own interests to Israeli needs, particularly when it comes to Iran.
"I am afraid that at some point Israel will also have to be sensitive to Indian concerns," he said. "We are not the 51st state of the United States, and for that matter we are also not an appendage or client state of Israel. We are friends, certainly. But vassals? No, sir."
"You cannot simply whistle and make our senior leaders go here and there, and ask us to sacrifice our interests," he said.
Bakshi specifically addressed possible pressure on India to distance itself from Iran because of the war.
"You cannot tell us: Throw Iran away because you are at war with it. When it comes to Iran, you cannot ask us to sacrifice our interests."
According to Bakshi, relations with Iran are vital to India economically and geostrategically as well. He pointed to the possibility of purchasing Iranian oil at low prices, refining it at Indian refineries, and subsequently exporting the products to other markets.
Beyond that, he stressed Iran's importance as an overland route for India.
"Iran provides India with the land bridge to Central Asia and the land bridge to Afghanistan, and these are of vital importance to us."
India cannot afford to give up those routes because of the war between Israel and Iran, he said.
"We cannot close these land routes because Israel is at war with Iran."
Bakshi concluded that the friendship between India and Israel remains important, but that from New Delhi's perspective, it has clear limits when major security and economic interests are at stake. Against the backdrop of growing ties between Turkey and Pakistan, and Indian concerns over a broader Sunni alliance, he believes that India's relationship with Iran is becoming more important, not less.

articles.title: Trump announces 'most crushing' economic war on Iran
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced the launch of an unprecedented "crushing economic operation" against Iran. Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the newly announced sanctions campaign as a diversion, warning that the "so-called 'Economic D-Day'" would only bring further defeat to Washington
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, during his two-day visit to Baghdad, said the US is seeking an "honourable exit" from the region while promoting a "new regional order"
Oil prices for Brent crude edged up to $91.87 a barrel
Israeli attacks on Gaza killed at least 10 Palestinians on Wednesday, including the police chief of the women’s department and several police officers, in an Israeli air strike on police headquarters
And so we continue our live coverage...
Yemen's Houthis say targeted Saudi airport, Aramco facility
Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Thursday that they targeted an airport and a facility belonging to state-owned oil giant Aramco in Saudi Arabia's southern Najran region, near the Yemeni border.
The group "successfully carried out two military operations using drones: the first targeted a sensitive Saudi enemy site at Najran Airport, while the second targeted the Aramco facility in Najran", military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on Telegram.
Earlier on Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards had warned that Saudi Arabia would be "unable to contain" the Houthis as the rebels ramp up attacks on the kingdom.
This week, a Yemeni minister told AFP that the Houthi rebels were plotting to seize land along the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which would allow them to further threaten the vital shipping artery.
Three Houthi military sources, as well as a spokesman for the Yemeni government forces battling them near the waterway, also told AFP the rebels were planning to advance south from their current territory.
Turkey denies military visit to Syria air base hit by Israel
Turkey on Thursday denied having any military presence at an air base in north Syria struck by Israel earlier this week, and vowed to continue "resolutely" supporting Syrian sovereignty.
The denial came two days after Syria accused Israel of hitting a disused military air base near the northwestern city of Aleppo that was damaged during the civil war and has been out of service since 2012.
Israel said a Turkish military delegation had recently visited the site, with a Syrian war monitor saying it was part of efforts to reactivate the base.
"There was no Turkish military delegation at the Abu al-Zuhur airbase before or during the attack carried out by Israel," a defence official told journalists, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu's office also said Turkish forces had recently toured the base, with the prime minister himself warning that Israel would not tolerate a "threat" from a Turkish presence there.
Vatican says 'serious concerns' over Israel-Lebanon deal
The Vatican expressed "serious concerns" Thursday about problems implementing a US-brokered deal between Israel and Lebanon, following a meeting between Pope Leo XIV and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun.
During a private, 30-minute audience at the Vatican, Aoun had urged the pontiff to support Beirut's push to secure the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon envisaged by the deal, the Lebanese presidency said.
"The Holy See, whilst welcoming the signing of the document, has expressed serious concerns about the difficulties being encountered in implementing it, and has pledged its support for efforts to that end," the Vatican said in a statement.
Despite an agreement, Israel has kept up strikes that have killed women and children, and persists in heavy demolition operations in south Lebanon.
Its forces are occupy a strip of territory around 10 kilometres (six miles) deep inside the Lebanese border.
At the Vatican, Aoun also met with the Holy See's second-in-command, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, and its top diplomat, Paul Richard Gallagher.
It was the second private audience between Pope Leo and Aoun at the Vatican.
Although the Islamabad MoU was intended to give Washington and Tehran 60 days for talks, the two sides have failed to achieve a diplomatic breakthrough.
At this point, the US-Iran confrontation is entering a new period which will likely be shaped by continued sanctions, pressure around the Strait of Hormuz, threats, negotiations, and limited military activity.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that the USS George Washington is now deployed in the Middle East, after the lengthy deployment of US personnel onboard the USS Lincoln sparked critique and a crisis.
“The George Washington Carrier Strike Group is operating in Middle East during a scheduled deployment after arriving in the CENTCOM theater yesterday,” it said in a statement posted on X.
Turkey, Egypt, Qatar condemn Israeli strikes on Gaza
In a joint statement, Turkey, Egypt and Qatar "strongly condemned" recent Israeli attacks across Gaza that have killed at least 15 Palestinians in less than a day.
They also expressed "deep concern" over Israel's "ongoing violations".
Oman: lasting security in Hormuz requires regional peace
Oman said lasting security in the Strait of Hormuz required permanent peace in the region and rejected further escalation or conflict, its foreign minister told his Japanese counterpart on Thursday.
Iran has said a deal with Oman on new shipping lanes through the strait was in its final stages.
Oil prices jumped around 2.5 percent as peace talks between the US and Iran remained stalled, with Tehran keeping the key Strait of Hormuz shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
US President Donald Trump pledged "economic warfare" against Tehran and threatened any country that trades with it, further dimming hopes of an imminent deal to end nearly six months of war in the Gulf.
Iran on Thursday executed an Afghan national convicted over the killing of police officers during anti-government demonstrations, the 30th in a wave of hangings since the start of the Middle East war, a rights group said.
Ghaem Hosseini was executed after being convicted of involvement in the deaths of four police officers, the Iranian judiciary's Mizan Online website reported.
It said he was a foreign national, without providing further details. But, the Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) group said the 21-year-old was from Afghanistan and was hanged at Isfahan central prison.
Mizan Online said Hosseini was convicted "of drawing a weapon and causing fear and terror, creating widespread insecurity, acting against people's physical integrity and national security in a manner that seriously disrupted public order".
But according to IHR, Hosseini was accused of kicking one of the policemen and the "authorities have presented no evidence proving that his actions led to the death of any of the policemen".
The case "is a stark example of collective punishment and the arbitrary use of the death penalty by the Islamic Republic," said IHR director Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam.
He is the fifth person to be hanged over the case involving the death in Isfahan of four policemen during the nationwide protests that peaked in January.
He is also the second Afghan national to be executed over the protests, after Gol Mohammad Mohammadi was hanged in the same case in July.
At least 12 defendants in the case have been sentenced to death, said IHR.
A tanker was boarded by six armed people who took control of the vessel and diverted it towards Somalia, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Thursday.
UKMTO earlier said it had received a report of an incident 136 nautical miles east of Yemen's Mukalla, where the tanker, travelling west in the Gulf of Aden, reported being approached by an unauthorised vessel.

Pakistan summons US diplomat after Trump envoy’s comments
Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the top US diplomat in Islamabad to lodge a “strong demarche” over remarks made by Washington’s ambassador in New Delhi that Jammu and Kashmir is an “important part of India.”
Sergio Gor, who is also the US special envoy to South and Central Asia, made the comments in Srinagar, the part of Kashmir administered by India, on Wednesday. Gor, a close confidant and former business partner of US President Donald Trump, is on a two-day trip to India’s Jammu and Kashmir state and the federally administered Ladakh region.
“Kashmir is an important part of India,” Gor told reporters after meeting Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. “It is an incredibly beautiful place.”
India and Pakistan, which gained independence when Britain partitioned its colonial territories in South Asia in 1947, have competing claims on Kashmir.
Hours after the comments, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Charge d’Affaires Natalie Baker – the top US envoy in Islamabad – and lodged a protest over Gor’s “factually incorrect remarks” and “irresponsible statement.”
“It was underscored that Jammu and Kashmir is an internationally recognized disputed territory, awaiting final disposition in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Nuclear-armed neighbors India and Pakistan clashed briefly with missiles and drones last year after 26 people were killed in a terror attack in Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi blamed on Pakistan-backed terror groups.
Gor’s comments have come despite a close rapport between Trump and Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir. Trump had claimed to have intervened to stop the India-Pakistan clash – an assertion that New Delhi dismissed. Islamabad, however, credited the US president with ending the short conflict and recommended him for the Nobel Peace Prize last year.
Trump has, in return, called Munir “my favorite field marshal.” Islamabad has also been acting as a mediator to end the Mideast war, which was triggered by US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

articles.title: Once again, Israeli air strikes are massacring people in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What ceasefire? Once again, Israeli air strikes are massacring people in Gaza
Israel attacked the Gaza Strip after days of contacts and meetings aimed at advancing the fragile ceasefire to its next stage, raising renewed fears that the truce could collapse and the war could return on a wider scale.
At least 15 Palestinians were killed and dozens injured by two Israeli airstrikes on Gaza City within less than 24 hours.
The first, on Tuesday evening, hit a beachside café in the port area. The second, on Wednesday afternoon, hit a municipal police headquarters in the city centre, killing at least nine people and injuring around 15 others, according to Palestinian medical sources.
The strikes came as US, Egyptian and Qatari mediators intensified efforts to advance negotiations over the second phase of the ceasefire agreement.
The talks remain stalled over several fundamental issues, including an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, Hamas's weapons, and the future administration and security of the territory.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that any future arrangement must guarantee Israel's security and has vowed that Israel would not leave Gaza.
Hamas, meanwhile, says the question of its disarmament cannot be separated from an end to the genocidal war, an Israeli withdrawal and guarantees that the agreement will be implemented.
Nine killed at police headquarters
At least nine Palestinians, including a woman, were killed on Wednesday afternoon when an Israeli airstrike struck the Hamas-run municipal police headquarters in central Gaza City.
The Gaza police force said Israeli aircraft targeted the headquarters, causing deaths and injuries.
Medical sources said some victims arrived at hospitals in pieces, while around 15 wounded people were being treated, several of them in critical condition.
Palestinian sources identified six of those killed as Brigadier General Abu Akram Jundiya, Colonel Abu Abdullah al-Hajin, Colonel Abu Khalil Tamraz, Major Abu Bilal Abu Sam'an, Colonel Abu Omar Aliyan and Colonel Faten al-Sahhar, who headed the women's police force in Gaza City. The identities of the remaining victims were still being verified.
Witnesses said the strike caused a powerful explosion and scattered shrapnel across the surrounding area.
The headquarters is located near a municipal park and tents sheltering displaced Palestinians, according to local sources.
Residents described scenes of panic following the blast, saying the area had been busy with civilian activity when the attack took place.
Gaza's Ministry of Interior and National Security accused Israel of carrying out a "brutal massacre" against members of the civilian police force and appealed to mediators and the international community to intervene.
"The occupation is working to dismantle the police force in order to spread chaos within Palestinian society," the ministry said.
Hamas described the strike as "a new Zionist war crime", saying it demonstrated the Netanyahu government's refusal to implement the ceasefire agreement and move towards its next phase.
The movement also rejected Israeli claims that attacks on police personnel were aimed at resistance leaders, calling such assertions a justification for targeting civilians and members of the police.
Less than a day earlier, another Israeli strike had killed six Palestinians at a café in Gaza City's port area.
Six people, including a child, were killed and 14 wounded when an Israeli airstrike hit the "Helwa wal Murra" café on Tuesday evening, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health and medical sources.
Ismail al-Thawabta, director general of Gaza's Government Media Office, said the victims were taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex.
Witnesses said the café was frequented by civilians and that the force of the explosion threw several people into the sea, prompting rescue teams to search the water.
The six killed were identified as Ezz El-Din Salem Deeb, Jihad Muhammad Hamdi Al-Masdi, Muhammad Hamdi Ahmad Al-Masri, Essam Muhammad Musa Murtaja, Muhammad Fathi Hussein Nasser and Samed Samir Harb Abu Habel.
The Israeli army claimed it had targeted "leaders in an elite Hamas unit during a meeting", including a company commander and three faction leaders.
It alleged that those targeted were involved in planning attacks against Israeli forces in Gaza and said one had participated in the 7 October 2023 attack.
A Hamas source, who preferred not to be named, told The New Arab that the members targeted at the café were unarmed and had been meeting as part of preparations to consolidate the movement's weapons and implement US President Donald Trump's plan.
The claim adds further sensitivity to the attack because Hamas's weapons remain one of the most contentious issues in negotiations over the next phase of the ceasefire.
Fears of more war
The recent increase in Israeli violence also extended beyond airstrikes. Local sources said an Israeli special forces unit carried out an operation in southern Gaza early Wednesday, arresting a senior Hamas police officer.
Witnesses in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis said a force of around 15 to 20 soldiers, accompanied by dogs, entered from the al-Shouka area and reached the tent of Colonel Sabri Abdelaal before arresting him along with Nash'at Za'arab, who works for a security company.
The force subsequently withdrew towards the Israeli-held "yellow line", according to the sources.
The operation, coinciding with the strike on the municipal police headquarters, has raised questions about Israel's approach to Gaza's security and police structures at a time when negotiators are discussing who will administer and police the territory during the next phase.
The recent violence occurred during a sensitive political time. US envoy Jared Kushner met Hamas officials in Cairo and then traveled to Israel for talks with Netanyahu, as Washington, Egypt, and Qatar urged parties to implement the second phase of the ceasefire.
Major disagreements remain: Israel demands Hamas's disarmament and security guarantees, while Hamas wants an end to the war and Israeli withdrawal before discussing weapons.
Netanyahu emphasises Israel's security, which Hamas sees as enabling future military action. Reports also say Netanyahu plans to meet opposition leader Yair Lapid to brief him on security issues amid mounting political and security pressures.
In Gaza, residents and analysts say the renewed attacks demonstrate how distant the language of ceasefire negotiations remains from reality on the ground.
Gaza-based political analyst Taysir Abdullah told TNA that Israel's use of high-explosive weapons in densely populated areas makes civilian casualties almost inevitable.
"What does the occupation expect when it launches a missile weighing a ton of explosives into the midst of displaced people's tents, whatever the justification or reason?" he said. "Yesterday, six were killed in Gaza's port, and today nine were killed in the municipal park. Does he think he's performing delicate surgery with a laser endoscope?"
"These are piles of tightly packed flesh. If you hit a small stone, you'd hit two or three people, so what about a missile?" he added.
Abdullah questioned whether the attacks could genuinely be described as targeted operations against wanted individuals, arguing that civilians continue to bear the consequences.
"These are massacres for which children, women, and the elderly pay the price daily," he said, warning that continued attacks during negotiations could undermine efforts to reach a durable agreement.
He also criticised Palestinian factions meeting in Cairo for what he described as passivity, urging them to take action rather than limiting themselves to statements of condemnation.
Between negotiations and bombardment
For Gaza's residents, the ceasefire remains an abstraction when explosions can return without warning.
"We don't understand how we can talk about a second phase, an agreement, and mediators, while at the same time we hear explosions and see people falling before our eyes," Gaza City resident Ibrahim Abu Shaaban told TNA.
"If negotiations are underway, who will stop the bombing? And who can guarantee that the agreement will hold if Israel can bomb whenever it wants?" he asked.
Another resident, Mohammed Odwan, said fear had returned to Gaza's streets.
"Every day we hear news about negotiations, then the bombing comes and kills people," he said. "For us, it makes no difference whether they say the war is over or it continues, as long as death reaches our tents, cafés and streets."

MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Pirates hijacked a Cameroon-flagged cargo ship off Somalia’s Puntland coast earlier this week and took the vessel, which was carrying Turkish weapons, toward the region’s Nugaal coast, a Somali official said Thursday.
The M/V LUTUF was seized on Monday about 3½ nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district, the official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity, because he wasn’t authorized to speak publicly about sensitive information.
The ship, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu, as well as communications and satellite equipment, the official said.
The 10-member crew included six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards, he said.
There was no immediate comment from Turkish authorities about the incident.
Eight pirates, believed to be members of a group previously involved in the hijacking of the M/V Sward on April 26, took the vessel toward the coast near Garmaal in Puntland’s Dangoroyo district.
Two Turkish-owned vessels later approached the hijacked ship, while Turkish helicopters and drones monitored the area, the official said. On Tuesday, a small boat carrying two men approached the vessel and delivered khat, a stimulant commonly chewed in Somalia, he said.
After the boat returned to shore, an airstrike followed, killing four men and wounding two others, the official said.
The circumstances of the strike, including who carried it out and whether those killed were involved in the hijacking, couldn’t immediately be independently verified. The status of the LUTUF, including its crew and cargo, wasn’t immediately clear. The AP couldn’t independently verify all details of the account.

Natalie Harp, special assistant to Donald Trump, continues to be the focus of media attention Thursday after an MS Now report revealed that she had worked at the White House for nearly a year without obtaining a security clearance.
Harp, a former One America News Network show host, has emerged as a key gatekeeper to the president. Her presence with Trump when the president left Air Force One as a decoy while sneaking on to another plane in a service cart – even as senior officials remained behind – drew attention.
Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator from Georgia, amplified that attention with comments at a rally Sunday in Atlanta. Speaking of Trump, Ossoff said: “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job; he wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie to their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”
A clip of his commentary went viral on social media, drawing attacks from the president’s defenders.
White House communications director Steven Cheung posted in reply on X: “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics,” while White House spokesman Davis Ingle posted, “Jon Ossoff is a cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama. Nobody gives a shit what this lightweight loser says.”
Ossoff marveled at the reaction to his observations in an interview Wednesday with Laurence O’Donnell on MS Now. “It’s been amazing to watch this White House melt down over this all week,” Ossoff said. “These White House staffers are adults, public officials paid by the taxpayer with immense power in positions of public trust. And whether it’s Natalie Harp printing out Donald Trump’s daily dose of delusion and flattery, or Peter Navarro steering taxpayer-funded loans to Trump family investments, or Pete Hegseth deluding the president daily into deepening this quagmire in the Middle East, no one cares about their feelings.”
The pile on continues: Rosie O’Donnell, a longstanding Trump antagonist filling in Wednesday night for Jimmy Kimmel, picked at the topic.

An FBI team seized electronic devices from former US representative Eric Swalwell at the San Francisco airport on Saturday, then raided his home in Washington, DC, the next day, CNN reported Thursday.
The raid is part of a federal investigation into the sexual assault allegations which ultimately drove the Bay Area Democrat to resign from office in April, sources familiar with the investigation told CNN. The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office and the Los Angeles Sheriff’s Department subsequently opened criminal investigations on Swalwell.
The White House released damaging declassified documents this week about Swalwell’s alleged relationship with Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese spy. The documents show that Swalwell told FBI agents in 2015 that he had had “physical relations” with Fang when she was campaigning on his behalf as an unpaid volunteer in 2012. Swalwell served on the House Select Committee on Intelligence when he spoke with the FBI in 2015, and remained so through their investigation, which did not result in charges.
A report by the San Francisco Chronicle on 10 April that Swalwell sexually assaulted an ex-staffer while she was too intoxicated to consent was followed by additional CNN reporting that surfaced three other women with detailed allegations of inappropriate conduct.
Historian Heather Cox Richardson weighed in on the attention that White House aide Natalie Harp has drawn over the last week.
In the most recent edition of Richardson’s “Letters from an American” newsletter, the Boston College history professor and popular writer took note of the strident attacks the White House made on CNN reporter Kristen Holmes after she asked Trump about comments on Harp made by Jon Ossoff at an Atlanta rally Sunday.
“You could almost feel the palpable relief that the White House might be able to gin up a controversy that could rally the base, one that, for the first time in a long time, didn’t automatically show the president or the administration in a bad light,” Richardson wrote. “Undermining Ossoff, whose speeches have been a particularly sharp thorn in the administration’s side lately, appeared to be icing on the cake.”
Richardson described the reaction as a “Streisand effect,” drawing additional attention to a subject conservatives might prefer to let lie, and “manufactured outrage” which distracts from the other topics Ossoff raised in the speech – Trump’s profiteering from his service in the White House, the consequences of the Iran war and rising prices for consumers.
A White House meeting on cryptocurrency and is amplifying a spike in bitcoin values Thursday.
President Donald Trump – who disclosed $1.4 billion in cryptocurrency earnings from his family’s investments in 2025 – is pushing congress to pass the CLARITY Act, which would define cryptocurrency as a commodity and move much of its regulation to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Bitcoin – along with gold and other commodities – began rising sharply in value at 10:30 Wednesday morning when the US treasury department announced it would double its long-end bond buybacks to at least $4 billion per operation, supporting market liquidity. Thursday morning, the CFTC’s Innovation Advisory Committee held its inaugural meeting to discuss the regulation of crypto assets, artificial intelligence, and prediction markets.
“America has long been the global hub of financial innovation,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “I look forward to meeting with the entrepreneurs, thinkers, and builders of the CFTC’s Innovation Advisory Committee to discuss ways emerging technologies and financial products are shaping our markets as we embark upon the new frontier of finance.”
The agenda includes discussion of agentic finance and the use of AI in derivatives markets, as well as the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.
The CLARITY Act faces questions from the banking industry, which does not want crypto assets to be able to offer interest payments, which is seen as undermining traditional banking deposits. Lawmakers also want better protections against the use of cryptocurrency in money laundering and to restrict officials – including Trump – from conflicts of interest in the crypto industry.
James Braid, the longest-serving legislative affairs director of Trump’s presidency, is leaving the White House ahead of the midterms. Braid navigated the cabinet confirmations of controversial appointees like that of Pete Hegseth at defense and Robert Kennedy Jr. at health and human services. He also shepherded the One Big Beautiful Bill Act through a congress with historically-tight margins for Republicans, while beating back war powers resolutions.
Republican lawmakers are acknowledging his service as he exits.

Trump cycled through four legislative directors in his first term. Michele Tafoya: from unassuming NFL sideline reporter to rightwing firebrand
Andrew Lawrence
As the third leg of NBC’s Sunday Night Football crew alongside play-by-play man Al Michaels and the tart-tongued analyst Cris Collinsworth, Michele Tafoya was a paragon of deference and neutrality for 11 years as an NFL sideline reporter, dutifully relating boilerplate tactics, talking points and injury updates when she wasn’t nodding along to softball interviews or fumbling through hammy production gimmicks for viewers who might have been too offline to get the bit.
She was almost pathologically committed to not doing anything to draw attention to herself or her gender in an era when sideline reporting was a fast track to national celebrity. (“New Orleans doesn’t want to lose to Atlanta twice in a season …”) Anyone who says they saw the 61-year-old emerging as a rightwing firebrand was watching a different game.

On Thursday, Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s minister of foreign affairs posted on X screenshots from various news outlets reporting that the US national debt had reached $40tnfor the first time in history.

US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”
Democrats and Republicans outraged over $40tn national debt
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of US politics.
The US gross national debt reached $40tn for the first time on Wednesday, the highest in US history.
The government deficit doubled over the past decade, with government spending growing under both Donald Trump and Joe Biden – Trump approved $8.4tn worth of debt during his first term, with a large chunk going to Covid-19 relief spending, while Biden approved $4.3tn worth of debt.
In fiscal year 2026, which began in October 2025, $1.8tn has been added to the debt so far.
Both Democrats and Republicans responded to the milestone with outrage, with Democrats placing the blame on Trump and a Republican-controlled Congress for the uptick in spending.
“The President said he’d pay off the debt in his first term. Well we all knew that was a lie. Instead he ran it up to $40 trillion while he and his family made billions,” Mark Kelly, a Democratic senator from Arizona, posted on X.
“Republicans ran up the tab, handed billionaires another tax break, and now wanna lecture working families about ‘fiscal responsibility’. You can’t max out the card AND pretend you’re the accountant. Pick a struggle,” Jasmine Crockett, a Democratic congresswoman from Texas, said.
“The Republican One Big Ugly Bill adds over $4 trillion alone—all to shamefully give tax breaks to billionaires and corporations,” Jason Crow, a Democratic congressman from Colorado, posted on X.

After Republican senator Rick Scottposted on X that “Congress needs to get spending under control”, netizens were quick to add that he had voted to pass this bill.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who regularly clashed with Trump and his own party as well as with his colleagues across the aisle, has long worn on his suit jacket a debt badge, a three-inch-long pin he created that updates the national debt in real time. “When I invented the debt badge, the national debt was just over $31 trillion,” he posted on X.

articles.body:
Russia unleashed a barrage of missiles and drones across Ukraine early Thursday, killing at least 13 people and wounding dozens more.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the hours-long attack struck Kyiv and the surrounding region as well as Odesa and Chernihiv, damaging apartment buildings, a children’s hospital and a school in the capital. articles.title: Russia faked broadcasts from Sweden’s national TV to smear its PM—the same network already hit Germany and France this month
articles.body:
Russia's Matryoshka bot network has launched disinformation campaigns targeting elections in Sweden, Germany, and France this month, fabricating video clips branded with the logos of trusted European media outlets, Sweden's national public broadcaster SVT reported. Analysts in multiple countries found the campaign aims not to reach mass audiences but to overwhelm newsrooms' fact-checking capacity.
Fake clips target Swedish PM weeks before the vote
Seven fabricated video clips appeared on the social media platform X within a single hour on 18 August. Among them were clips branded with the logos of SVT and the Swedish newspaper Dagens Nyheter. Others hijacked the visual branding of Euronews and Germany's Der Spiegel. None were ever produced by these outlets.
The fake videos spread lies about election fraud in Sweden and directed false accusations at Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson personally. Sweden holds general elections on 13 September.
"We see this all over Europe. Russians target countries that support Ukraine," Kristersson told SVT.
Russian opposition analysis group Antibot4navalny linked the posts to Matryoshka, a pro-Russian influence campaign named after the Russian nesting doll.
Also known as Operation Overload and Storm-1679, Matryoshka was first exposed by Antibot4navalny in 2024 and is one of several Kremlin-linked disinformation networks alongside the Doppelgänger campaign and Storm-1516. A previous SVT review found the majority of Matryoshka's posts aimed to influence Western support for Ukraine.
Sweden says it stopped Russian operation to discredit country and EU. But no one will be prosecuted
Campaign targets newsrooms, not audiences
The fabricated posts rarely get more than a few hundred or a few thousand genuine views, Antibot4navalny told SVT. Analysts say the campaign is not primarily designed to reach a large audience. Matryoshka operators actively push fabricated posts to journalists and fact-checkers, often disguising them as verification requests. A 2024 report by France's state anti-disinformation body Viginum suggested the campaign aims to distract and overload newsrooms' fact-checking resources through large volumes of targeted requests. In posts targeting Sweden, the network tagged the social media accounts of several outlets, including SVT and Dagens Nyheter.
The campaign may also seek to generate media coverage that amplifies its message or makes it appear more influential than it is, the think tank ISD assessed.
Sweden detains Russians who “camped” near home of CEO of Gripen jets Ukraine is buying
Germany and France targeted the same month
On 12 August, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), warned that Matryoshka is targeting local and regional elections in Germany scheduled for September. In early August, France's Viginum detected a Matryoshka operation directed at presidential candidate Gabriel Attal ahead of the 2027 vote. French prosecutors opened a probe into the campaign on 18 August.
In April, the network promoted false claims of Ukraine's involvement in the assassination attempt on US President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Six UK pro-Palestine orgs demand end of arms trade to Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
On anniversary of 'symbolic' Palestine recognition, UK groups demand end to Israel arms trade
With the first anniversary of Britain's official recognition of the State of Palestine approaching, six British pro-Palestinian organisations have stepped up pressure on the government, calling for an end to the arms trade with Israel, the suspension of military and intelligence support, and comprehensive sanctions against it.
The demands come alongside calls for British action that goes beyond political recognition to practical measures.
In a comment to The New Arab on Wednesday, 19 August, Chris Nineham, vice-president of the Stop the War Coalition, said Britain's recognition of Palestine "was welcome, but, as we feared, it was symbolic", adding, "The people of Palestine need action, and we are calling on our government to end British support for Israel immediately.
"We are working to organise another mass demonstration on 10 October to pressure it to take action."
Nineham's comments come as the organisations prepare to organise a new national march in central London next October, in an attempt to pressure the British government to take tougher steps towards Israel.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, the organisations said that "Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face killing, hunger and displacement, while British-funded humanitarian aid remains subject to Israeli restrictions".
They called on the British government to work to halt Israeli attacks and ensure aid reaches the Strip without restrictions.
The demand to lift restrictions on aid coincides with a position Britain announced at the UN Security Council on 11 August, when it called on the Israeli authorities to end what it described as "unacceptable restrictions" on aid and allow safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza.
'Britain must act'
The statement is titled, "Three years of genocide... Britain must act".
The signatories said their next march will take place on Saturday, 10 October, at noon in central London, coinciding with three years since the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
The official website of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign confirms the date and location of the march.
The statement was signed by the Palestinian Forum in Britain, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, the Stop the War Coalition, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Friends of Al-Aqsa, and the Muslim Association of Britain.
The United Kingdom officially recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September 2025.
At the time, the government said that the decision aimed to revive hope for peace and a two-state solution.
But the organisations that signed the statement believe the recognition was not followed by British action at the required level.
They say "real action" requires ending arms trade with Israel and suspending military and intelligence support that they consider to contribute to facilitating violations of international law.
They also called for British companies, banks, universities and charities to be prevented from supporting activities linked to the occupation or settlements, starting with a ban on trade connected to Israel's illegal occupation and extending to comprehensive sanctions against Israel.
Britain suspended 29 export licences to Israel in September 2024 after concluding that there was a clear risk that the equipment covered by them could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
The latest government data shows that six additional licences were subsequently suspended or amended as new information emerged.
The organisations expanded their demands to include the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, warning of continued settlement expansion, settler violence and restrictions on Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The British government, for its part, says Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
It recently condemned the rise in settler violence and expressed concern about developments at the Noble Sanctuary in Jerusalem.
In June, London, in coordination with international partners, imposed sanctions on six entities and one individual, saying they were involved in financing, enabling or carrying out acts of settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Britain also strengthened its guidance for British companies and citizens in June, explicitly advising them against engaging in economic or financial activities in Israeli settlements, which it considers illegal, while reaffirming its continued support for trade with Israel within its pre-1967 borders.
In their statement, the organisations said Britain's commitment to international law "cannot be held hostage to the Israeli electoral timetable", arguing that the time had come to move from political recognition of the Palestinian state to practical measures.
The organisers are calling for widespread participation in the 10 October march, in an attempt to put pressure back on the streets of Britain.
They also want to place the issues of arms, sanctions, trade and military support at the forefront of the debate over what has actually changed in British policy since the recognition of Palestine.

articles.title: Romania destroys naval drone near offshore gas platform
articles.body:
- Romania neutralized one maritime drone near the Neptun Deep gas platform on Thursday, hit first by an F-16 and later destroyed by EOD personnel.
- Authorities initially reported two separate drones before clarifying it was a single device that survived the F-16's cannon fire before being found and destroyed.
Romania neutralized a maritime drone near the Neptun Deep gas platform in the Black Sea on Thursday. Officials initially reported that two separate drones had been destroyed, but it was later established that only one drone was involved throughout the entire incident, according to Defense Minister Radu Miruță and Romanian President Nicușor Dan.
The drone was spotted several hundred meters from the platform’s gas extraction operations at around 6:28 a.m. local time, reported by a commercial vessel working in the area, according to Romania’s Ministry of National Defence. Two Romanian F-16s were scrambled, and one aircraft engaged the target with its onboard cannon. The drone was hit and damaged but not destroyed, and it continued drifting in the sea.
A Romanian Coast Guard vessel then arrived in the area to verify the results of the engagement. When the crew located the damaged drone, they initially believed they had found a second device. They had not. It was the same drone that had already been struck by the F-16, still drifting after surviving the initial hit. Romanian EOD personnel subsequently destroyed it completely.
Miruță said the drone was loaded with explosives and that Ukraine had officially confirmed through a recently established direct communication channel that it did not belong to Ukrainian forces.
The drone was found within Romania’s exclusive economic zone, roughly 80 nautical miles east of Constanța, near the offshore platform where several hundred people were working at the time.
President Dan congratulated the armed forces and the F-16 pilots, crediting the Coast Guard for its speed in reporting the drone’s presence.
“A race against time, in which the top priority was protecting the lives of the people working on the platform and keeping critical infrastructure out of any potential danger,” Dan said.
“I strongly condemn the escalation of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation,” Dan said. “We remain vigilant alongside our NATO allies to defend ourselves and repel such provocations.”
Thursday’s incident follows a pattern of drone activity around the Neptun Deep project in recent weeks. Ukrainian long-range drones struck an oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan, marking another attack on Russia’s refining industry just a day after a key processing unit was hit at a major refinery in Ufa, according to the Exilenova+ OSINT community on August 20.

One video captured the moment of an apparent impact on the refinery grounds. Preliminary OSINT assessments identified the targeted facility as the TANECO oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk.
TANECO is one of Russia’s newest and largest refining facilities and is considered a strategic asset of Russian oil producer Tatneft. The complex produces more than 20 types of petroleum products.
Its output includes gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, base oils, marine fuel, and other refined petroleum products. The refinery has a reported oil-processing depth of up to 99%, allowing it to extract a particularly high share of usable products from crude oil.
Authorities in Tatarstan issued an air raid warning over the threat of drones at around 3:30 am, with Nizhnekamsk among the areas specifically warned of a possible attack.
The latest strike comes as Ukraine continues targeting Russian refining infrastructure in an effort to reduce the production of fuel used by the Russian military and broader economy. Damage to critical refinery equipment can force operators to reduce crude-processing volumes and put additional pressure on domestic fuel supplies.
The Nizhnekamsk attack followed another strike on Russia’s oil industry only a day earlier.
During the previous attack, Ukrainian drones struck the ELOU-AVT-6 unit at the Bashneft-Ufa Oil Refinery, a key piece of equipment responsible for crude oil desalting and primary fractionation.
The unit can process more than 6 million metric tons of crude oil annually.
Primary fractionation separates crude into products including kerosene, gasoline components, diesel fractions, and fuel oil, which are then sent to secondary processing units for further refining into finished fuels.
Bashneft-UNPZ is the oldest of Ufa’s three major refineries. The other two are Bashneft-Novoil and Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim, all of which are part of Russia’s Rosneft-controlled refining network.

articles.title: Hypersonic missile maker Castelion valued at $13 billion after raise
articles.body:
- Castelion raised $1 billion in Series C funding, valuing the hypersonic missile maker at $13 billion, with equity led by JPMorganChase, Andreessen Horowitz and Carlyle.
- The funding will expand production of Castelion's Blackbeard missile, fund a longer-range strike weapon, and develop new air and missile defense systems, with Blackbeard fielding targeted for 2027.
Castelion, a hypersonic missile developer based in Torrance, California, has raised $1 billion in a Series C funding round that values the company at $13 billion.
The round includes $800 million in equity financing and $250 million in committed financing for a revolving credit facility, the company said Aug. 19. JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group, Andreessen Horowitz and Carlyle co-led the equity portion. Lightspeed Venture Partners, Lavrock Ventures, Altimeter, General Catalyst and Interlagos also participated, along with new investor T. Rowe Price Associates.
The money will fund three efforts: expanding production of Castelion’s Blackbeard missile, developing a longer-range strike weapon, and building air and missile defense systems that draw on Blackbeard’s manufacturing methods.
Blackbeard is Castelion’s first hypersonic strike missile. The company has taken it from initial design to program of record in under four years, with fielding targeted for 2027. Castelion has secured more than $500 million in U.S. military contracts over the past 18 months, according to the company.
Production is centered at Castelion’s Project Ranger campus in Sandoval County, New Mexico, a 1,000-acre site the company describes as the largest dedicated hypersonic missile manufacturing facility in the country. Castelion had already committed more than $250 million in private infrastructure spending there and plans to commit hundreds of millions more to expand manufacturing capacity. The company also has operations in Texas and California, along with an office in Washington, D.C.
The longer-range strike weapon has been in development at Castelion for several years and will use components and manufacturing techniques from Blackbeard, the company said. No range, cost or fielding timeline was disclosed. The planned defensive systems are intended to bring higher production rates and greater magazine depth to air and missile defense, according to Castelion, though the company did not specify a program name or timeline.
“Deterrence depends on unapologetic American strength: highly capable weapon systems that adversaries fear produced in quantities they can’t imagine at a price taxpayers can afford,” said Bryon Hargis, co-founder and CEO of Castelion.
“Castelion is helping to address a critical national security challenge by bringing greater speed, agility and manufacturing capacity to the development of next-generation defense technologies,” said Todd Combs, head of the Strategic Investment Group for JPMorganChase’s Security and Resiliency Initiative.
“We backed Castelion when it was a small team that wanted to build what the department of War most needed faster and cheaper than the experts thought possible,” said Katherine Boyle, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz. “Four years later there is a factory in New Mexico and a production agreement with the Department of War.”
Lightspeed’s Ravi Mhatre said his firm has invested in every Castelion funding round since leading its Series A, before the company had flown a complete system. “Three rounds later the company is mixing its own propellant in New Mexico and shipping hardware to the services,” he said.
Castelion was founded by Hargis along with Sean and Andrew, according to T. Rowe Price’s Emma Norchet, who cited the company’s existing contracts and self-funded manufacturing campus as factors in the investment decision.

articles.title: Russian drones threaten civilians and aid work in Ukraine, UN aid chief warns
articles.body:
Tom Fletcher said the UN needs more than €1.7 billion for its prioritised humanitarian response in Ukraine this year, with winter among his biggest concerns.
The intensifying use of drones against civilians and humanitarian workers is a dangerous obstacle for aid operations in Ukraine, the UN's humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, said on Wednesday.
Fletcher spoke to the Associated Press news agency in an interview after a visit to the southern city of Kherson, where he witnessed how communities are coping while living under the constant threat of Russian drone strikes.
Fletcher described the visit to Kherson, split by the Dnipro River which acts as an active front line, as “quite chilling."
Russian forces occupy the eastern bank, while Ukrainian forces hold the western bank. From across the water, surveillance and exploding drones routinely hunt and attack civilians, vehicles and public transit.
“It really gives us an insight into the dangers ahead of us,” he said.
The threat is also making it harder for humanitarian organisations to reach people who need assistance.
Fletcher spoke after attending a commemoration for two humanitarian workers who had died while doing their jobs.
“Drones are a real threat to not just civilians but the humanitarians who are here to protect them,” Fletcher said.
He said that aid workers are protected under international humanitarian law and yet marked humanitarian vehicles have still been hit. “So that does restrict what we can do," he said.
Local organisations are particularly exposed. More than two-thirds of operations funded through Ukraine's humanitarian fund are carried out by local groups, according to Fletcher.
“They’re the ones who are saying most loudly to us, we’re not protected,” he said.
Fletcher said the UN needs more than $2 billion (€1.7 billion) for its prioritised humanitarian response in Ukraine this year, with winter among his biggest concerns.
Damage to civilian infrastructure, including electricity, water and gas systems, could once again leave millions vulnerable during the harsh winter months, raising fears of a repeat of last winter’s severe conditions.
The UN has sharply narrowed its humanitarian priorities all over the world as donor funding has fallen.
Fletcher said the organisation initially identified 87 million people facing the most severe humanitarian needs, but that figure has since risen to about 92 million with the onslaught of Ebola in Africa, the earthquake in Venezuela and other conflicts.
The UN is seeking $23 billion (€19 billion) to provide life-saving assistance to those people and had raised about $11 billion (€9.4 billion), Fletcher said.
Ukraine is relatively well funded compared with many other crises, he added, with roughly 70%–75% of its hyper-prioritised funding requirement covered. But even full funding of the humanitarian plan would address only part of Ukraine’s needs.
A more selfish world
Fletcher also admitted that raising money for humanitarian operations has become more difficult as governments have increasingly redirected spending toward defence and domestic priorities.
“We’re in a more transactional world, I would say a more selfish world,” he said.
Fletcher said the UN now has to demonstrate that it is using limited taxpayer money efficiently and strategically.
“We have to show governments that we are spending their taxpayers’ money sensibly, wisely, in a prioritised way,” he said.
In a stark new assessment released on Wednesday, the UN warned that 907 aid workers were victims of violence last year and over 1,000 had been killed in three years.
Fletcher said he could not reassure colleagues that those responsible would be held accountable based on how the international community has reacted.
He said accountability should extend beyond identifying the person who physically carried out an attack.
“I want to see investigations into the people who fired the weapon or flew the drone,” he said.

articles.title: Bradley IFVs won battles in Ukraine. The parts to keep them running went out of production
articles.body:
The US Army Contracting Command—Detroit Arsenal has published a market survey seeking companies that can supply components for M2A2 ODS-SA Bradley infantry fighting vehicles (IFVs) headed to Ukraine—parts that original manufacturers have stopped making. The posting asks for firms with immediate access to the components or a realistic plan to restart their production, Militarnyi reported.
Maintaining Western armored vehicles in active combat has strained repair chains throughout the war, with licensing requirements and long lead times slowing restoration of battle-damaged equipment. When components go out of production entirely, the problem shifts from delayed repairs to no repairs at all.
Parts nobody makes
The survey targets components affected by what the command calls an aging manufacturing base. Original suppliers have discontinued production of multiple subsystems, including turret drive control units, transmission control modules, heater mounts, ammunition chutes, specialized Dialight Corp lens assemblies, and other structural, electrical, and mechanical parts unique to the M2A2 ODS-SA.
The posting is not a tender and does not guarantee a contract. Its stated goal is to identify companies that can either deliver the parts now or credibly restart production.
Restoring and sustaining Bradleys for Ukraine
The parts shortage creates a two-stage problem. Before Bradleys can be shipped to Ukraine, the US military refurbishes them at its depots—restoring each vehicle to combat-ready condition under a standard called Fully Mission Capable + Safety. Without the discontinued components, that refurbishment stalls.
The same parts are also needed to keep Bradleys already fighting in Ukraine on the road. The posting specifies that field servicing must proceed without delays caused by parts shortages—meaning the crisis affects both the pipeline into Ukraine and the fleet already there.
Potential contractors must demonstrate repair and technical validation capabilities, supply chain management, and the ability to quickly resume manufacturing of parts that no longer have a producer. The command requires a detailed transition plan with a timeline from contract signing to the delivery of the first restored vehicle.
The US also plans to involve the future contractor in training Ukrainian military mechanics. The contractor would develop courses, manuals, and provide specialized tools and equipment—including instruction on armored recovery vehicles.
The 25-mm cannon, stops T-72s, if the turret still turns
The M2 Bradley carries infantry into combat and mounts a 25-mm M242 Bushmaster cannon that fires up to 500 rounds per minute and can defeat Russian light armored vehicles and the side and rear armor of main battle tanks. The US has supplied more than 200 Bradleys to Ukraine under the previous administration, with combat losses mounting across multiple frontline sectors.
Separately, the US Army presented XM30 infantry fighting vehicle candidates at the Michigan Defense Expo 2026—the program is eventually designed to replace the Bradley.

articles.title: Trump 'serious' about direct Hezbollah talks to end Lebanon war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump 'serious' about direct Hezbollah talks to end Lebanon war
US President Donald Trump is prepared to hold direct talks with Hezbollah if they could help end the conflict in Lebanon, according to the head of a US-Lebanese advocacy group visiting Beirut.
Edward Gabriel, president of the American Task Force on Lebanon (ATFL) and a former US ambassador, told local television station Al Jadeed that members of his delegation had discussed the issue with US officials at the embassy in Beirut.
He said they were told Trump was "serious" about the possibility of direct dialogue with Hezbollah.
However, Gabriel said Washington did not currently believe the group had shown sufficient willingness to enter such talks.
"The United States believes that Hezbollah is not yet serious enough about having this conversation," he told Al Jadeed.
Direct US talks with Hezbollah would mark a significant shift in Washington's longstanding approach towards the Iran-backed group, which is alsodesignated as a terrorist organisation by the United States.
The comments came during a visit to Beirut by a bipartisan delegation of US congressional staff organised by ATFL, which advocates stronger political, economic and security ties between the US and Lebanon.
Lebanese MP Fouad Makhzoumi, who hosted the delegation at a dinner attended by several MPs, said the presence of congressional staff made the visit more significant than previous ATFL trips.
"They are the people appointed by the House and Senate, and they usually write reports and formulate positions," Makhzoumi told Al-Modon.
He said information gathered during the meetings would be turned into reports and assessments on the delegation's return to Washington and could feed into congressional discussions on aid, support for the Lebanese army and broader US policy towards Lebanon.
"This is not a ceremonial visit," Makhzoumi said. "They came to understand how serious Lebanon is about implementing the agreement, how the army can be supported, what problems exist and how far reforms have progressed."
The delegation included Republican and Democratic congressional staffers, some linked to the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
It met President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Lebanese Armed Forces commander General Rodolphe Haykal, as well as ministers and MPs.
Discussions focused heavily on the implementation of security arrangements in Lebanon, including Hezbollah's weapons, the role of the Lebanese army, verification mechanisms and the sequencing of disarmament and reconstruction.
Speaking to Al Jadeed, Gabriel said there was broad convergence between Beirut and Washington over the objective of disarmament, although substantial difficulties remained over implementation.
He expressed confidence that the Lebanese army could take on additional responsibilities and deploy to further "pilot areas" when conditions allowed, while stressing the need for continued US support for the armed forces.
Lebanese officials have argued that progress on bringing weapons under state control must be accompanied by reciprocal Israeli measures, including withdrawal from Lebanese territory.
Gabriel said Israel could not avoid addressing the issue.
"Israel has to address the issue of withdrawal from Lebanese territory, because the level of killing and destruction so far has become far too great," he told Al Jadeed.
He also praised President Aoun's previous call for direct talks with Israel, describing it as a "bold step".
"Lebanon had no other choice but that, or to face further destruction," Gabriel said.

articles.title: Ukraine’s top military marketplace has processed $235 million in orders. Now it goes further, letting units spec a custom drone across 17 characteristics
articles.body:
Ukrainian units can now tell drone makers exactly what they need and have it built. A new tool on the state defense-technology marketplace Brave1 Market lets military units order custom drones with defined specifications for specific battlefield needs, not only serial models, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.
Russia's war has pushed Kyiv to rebuild military procurement from the ground up, trading slow bureaucratic pipelines for digital platforms where frontline units pick and receive their own weapons faster. Brave1 has already processed over $235 million in orders.
The new tool turns Ukraine's drone procurement from a catalog-based system into a made-to-order one. Where units once chose from ready-made drones, they can now specify what they need across more than 17 characteristics and have makers compete to build it.
How the custom orders work
A unit defines the drone it wants. It submits a request specifying the required characteristics, quantity, and desired delivery timelines, selecting from parameters such as communication type, camera specifications, payload weight, and flight duration.
The manufacturer does not receive information about which unit made the request, and the system automatically sends the request to potential suppliers, who can submit offers or decline to participate. Keeping the requesting unit anonymous prevents makers from favoring or identifying particular units and keeps the competition on the drone itself.
Makers compete on price
When offers match, the system runs an auction. If several manufacturers propose solutions with identical characteristics, the system launches an automatic bidding process, and the lowest-priced offer wins. A military unit can then conclude a direct agreement with the maker, according to the Defense Ministry.
The mechanism drives cost down while meeting the spec. By pitting makers against each other on price once they meet the required characteristics, the system gets units the drone they specified at the lowest available cost, then lets them contract the winner directly, cutting out intermediaries.
